finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the q query parameter is interpolated into an f-string and passed to db.execute, allowing a UNION-based read of any table in shop.db.
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") at app.py:12

trace.note: term concatenated into SQL string inside a quoted LIKE pattern
jsonify(rows) returns attacker-chosen result rows to the caller

finding.guards_checked: None. No escaping, allow-list, length limit, or parameter binding on the path. Stacked statements are expected to be blocked by Python sqlite3 execute() single-statement restriction (not tested). Possible ATTACH DATABASE escalation is unverified. Exploitation was not executed: scratch reproduction script was denied.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:11 reads q from request.args with no validation; app.py:12 interpolates it into the SQL string with no parameter binding, escaping, or allowlist; app.py:9 /search has no auth decorator, and the directory contains only app.py, so there is no before_request hook or middleware. The sqlite3 single-statement restriction does not block a UNION SELECT, which is one statement, so the read-any-table claim holds.
verdict.reason: Anonymous callers reach /search (app.py:9), and the q value flows unparameterized from app.py:11 into the f-string SQL at app.py:12 and back out through jsonify at app.py:13, so a UNION-based read of other tables is possible with no effective control.

finding.claim: Possible broken access control in /by-owner: any anonymous caller can list all products for an arbitrary client-supplied owner value, with no check that the caller is that owner. Finding only if owner-to-product mappings are meant to be private.
finding.sink: db.execute("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE owner = ?", (owner,)) at app.py:25 returning product rows at app.py:26

trace.note: owner taken from client query string, no authentication
products filtered by attacker-chosen owner, parameterized (not SQLi)
jsonify(rows) returns product ids and names for that owner

finding.guards_checked: Query is parameterized, so no SQL injection. No authentication, session, or identity binding between caller and owner. Severity depends on whether owner mappings are intended to be public.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only control is the parameterized query at app.py:25, which blocks SQL injection but not unauthorized access. No authentication, session, or owner-identity check exists anywhere in app.py, and the route at app.py:22-26 is reachable anonymously.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (app.py:24 takes owner from the query string, app.py:25 filters by it, app.py:26 returns id and name) and an anonymous caller reaches it with no guard, but whether this is a vulnerability depends on whether owner-to-product mappings are meant to be private, and nothing in app.py:1-27 shows that intent. The same app also serves /search (app.py:9-13) and /product/<pid> (app.py:16-19) without auth, which suggests a public catalog, though that is not proof.
